subject: Mechanistic sources of calibration degradation after instruction fine-tuning
prompt:
Topic: Mechanistic sources of calibration degradation after instruction fine-tuning

We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-265)
response:
The central question is: why does a model that was well-calibrated after pretraining or RLHF become overconfident (or sometimes underconfident) once you fine-tune it on instruction-following data? The key concepts are epistemic calibration (whether a model's stated confidence tracks its actual accuracy), logit geometry (how fine-tuning shifts the distribution of output probabilities), exposure bias from curated datasets (instruction datasets are heavily filtered toward confident, assertive responses), and the mismatch between RLHF reward signals and calibration objectives (human raters tend to reward fluency and confidence, not hedging). A naive view treats calibration as a static property that survives fine-tuning unless you actively break it; the expert worry is that calibration degrades as a structural byproduct of the training objective itself — cross-entropy loss on demonstration data pushes the model toward high-probability mass on "correct-sounding" outputs regardless of whether the model's internal representations actually support certainty. More specifically, experts worry about label sharpness in instruction datasets: when every fine-tuning example is a clean question–answer pair with no uncertainty expressed, the model learns a prior that questions have definite answers, which collapses the probability mass it would otherwise spread across genuinely ambiguous outputs. The subtler issue is that you can't easily detect this from held-out loss curves — the model can simultaneously get better at the fine-tuning task and worse at knowing when it doesn't know, with no obvious signal in standard training metrics.

prompt:
What specific property of the cross-entropy loss function makes it structurally biased toward producing overconfident outputs, even when the training data itself contains uncertainty?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-266)
response:
Cross-entropy loss minimization is equivalent to maximum likelihood estimation over the training distribution, which means the optimal solution under infinite data is to exactly reproduce the empirical label distribution — but with finite, curated instruction data, the "empirical distribution" is a set of one-hot targets, and the loss actively penalizes probability mass placed on anything other than the single demonstrated answer. This creates a sharpening pressure: the gradient always points toward concentrating more mass on the target token, so the only equilibrium is a degenerate spike, and the regularization mechanisms (dropout, weight decay, early stopping) merely slow the approach to that spike rather than redirecting toward calibrated uncertainty. Guo et al. (2017, "On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks") showed this concretely for image classifiers — networks trained longer with cross-entropy became monotonically more overconfident even as accuracy plateaued, with ECE (Expected Calibration Error) worsening from ~2% to ~10% simply by training more epochs on the same data. For language models, the problem is compounded because instruction fine-tuning datasets (FLAN, Alpaca, ShareGPT derivatives) strip away naturally occurring uncertainty markers from source documents — a Wikipedia sentence hedged with "it is generally believed" becomes a fine-tuning target of confident assertion. The loss has no term that rewards the model for outputting a low-confidence answer when the ground truth is ambiguous; it only rewards matching the demonstrated token sequence, so uncertainty in the world is invisible to the objective unless it was explicitly encoded in the demonstration, which it almost never is. Anthropic's work on model-written evaluations and OpenAI's work on GPT calibration both note this asymmetry: the loss function can distinguish "wrong answer" from "right answer" but cannot distinguish "confidently right" from "appropriately uncertain."

subject: Mechanistic sources of calibration degradation after instruction fine-tuning
prompt:
Given that temperature scaling can recalibrate a model post-hoc without retraining, what does it mean that temperature scaling works — what does that reveal about where the calibration information is actually stored in the model?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-267)
response:
Temperature scaling works by dividing the final logits by a scalar T before the softmax, and the fact that a single scalar — fit on maybe a few thousand validation examples — substantially recovers calibration tells you something precise: the model's rank ordering of probabilities is already correct, but the magnitudes are systematically too extreme. This means the model's penultimate-layer representations (the pre-softmax logit vector) already encode genuine uncertainty — the relative relationships between candidate answers reflect something real about the model's internal evidence — but the fine-tuning process has applied a global compression toward high-confidence outputs that can be approximately undone by a uniform rescaling. Guo et al. (2017) showed T values of roughly 1.5–2.5 were sufficient to bring ECE from ~10% down to ~1–2% on ResNets, and similar T ranges appear in LLM calibration work, which is a striking finding: the distortion introduced by training is nearly affine in logit space, not some complex nonlinear corruption of the representations. The expert interpretation is that calibration is stored in the geometry of the logit manifold, not destroyed by fine-tuning — the relative distances between outputs are preserved, only the overall "sharpness" of the distribution changes, suggesting fine-tuning acts more like a global contrast enhancement on the probability landscape than like a rewriting of the underlying knowledge. The alarming implication, noted by Kadavath et al. (2022, "Language Models (Mostly) Know What They Know") is that this is only true on average — temperature scaling is a global fix for a problem that is actually heterogeneous across domains, so it recalibrates easy questions well while leaving hard or out-of-distribution questions still badly miscalibrated. This heterogeneity is what temperature scaling cannot fix: a single scalar T cannot simultaneously correct a model that is overconfident on factual recall questions (needs high T) and underconfident on common-sense reasoning questions (needs low T), meaning the residual miscalibration after temperature scaling clusters precisely in the cases that matter most.

prompt:
If the logit geometry largely survives fine-tuning but calibration degrades, does that imply the model's verbal expressions of uncertainty (saying "I'm not sure") and its probabilistic expressions of uncertainty (output token probabilities) are computed by different mechanisms — and if so, which one should we actually trust?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-268)
response:
Yes, the evidence strongly supports that these are dissociable mechanisms. Verbal uncertainty expressions are generated as next-token predictions conditioned on the conversational context — they are learned behaviors shaped by instruction fine-tuning data, where "I'm not sure" appears in specific pragmatic contexts (hedging before a guess, declining a request) and the model learns to produce them as stylistic outputs rather than as readouts of internal state. Token probabilities, by contrast, reflect the raw logit geometry over the vocabulary at each decoding step, which as we established survives fine-tuning in its rank structure. Kadavath et al. (2022) tested this dissociation directly by asking models to explicitly state their confidence as a probability ("P(True)") and comparing it to the implicit token-probability calibration — they found the verbalized probabilities were better calibrated than token probabilities for factual questions on Claude and GPT-class models, but only when the model was directly prompted to self-assess, suggesting the verbal channel can sometimes aggregate internal evidence more coherently than the raw output distribution. However, Xiong et al. (2023, "Can LLMs Express Their Uncertainty?") found the reverse in many settings: verbal confidence expressions are highly sensitive to prompt framing, persona, and sycophantic pressure, whereas token probabilities are relatively stable across paraphrases of the same question — a model told "a professor asks" gives more confident verbal hedges than one told "a student asks," while the underlying token probabilities barely shift. The practical answer is: neither is reliably trustworthy alone, but they fail in different directions — token probabilities are miscalibrated in magnitude but stable and manipulation-resistant, while verbal expressions are more contextually coherent but gameable and socially conditioned. The expert move is to use them as a consistency check: when verbal uncertainty and token-probability uncertainty strongly disagree on the same query, that disagreement is itself a signal that the model is in a regime where its self-knowledge is breaking down.

This dissociation is not merely theoretical — it is arguably the default outcome of standard RLHF pipelines. Human raters consistently reward hedging language as a signal of trustworthiness and intellectual honesty, so the reward model learns to score responses higher when they contain epistemic markers like "I think," "I'm not certain," or "you may want to verify this," independent of whether those markers correspond to actual uncertainty in the underlying token distribution. Simultaneously, the RLHF objective drives the policy toward high-probability, fluent completions that maximize expected reward — which means the token-level generation becomes more peaked and confident even as the surface text becomes more hedged, because confident fluent text with sprinkled hedges scores better than genuinely uncertain, halting, or low-probability text. Kalai and Vempala (2024, "Calibrated Language Models Must Hallucinate") formalize a version of this: any model optimized to produce fluent, human-preferred text faces structural pressure toward overconfidence at the token level because low-probability outputs are penalized by both cross-entropy and reward maximization, creating a ratchet that verbal hedges cannot counteract. The concrete mechanism is a decoupling of surface pragmatics from generative confidence: the model learns "insert hedge token here" as a stylistic rule triggered by certain question types (recent events, specialized domains, contested facts) while the softmax distribution over the actual answer tokens remains sharply peaked, so you get "I'm not entirely sure, but I believe the answer is X" with P(X) ≈ 0.97. This is detectable empirically by comparing ECE on the answer tokens conditioned on the presence versus absence of verbal hedges — if the model were well-calibrated, hedged answers should show lower token-level confidence, but in RLHF-tuned models this correlation is weak or absent, which has been noted informally in evaluations of GPT-4 and Claude-class models though rigorous published numbers remain sparse.

If RLHF reward models are themselves neural networks trained on human preference data, do they inherit and amplify the same calibration pathologies as the policy models they train — and what does a miscalibrated reward model specifically do to the policy's uncertainty structure?

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-270)
response:
Reward models absolutely inherit calibration pathologies, and the pipeline compounds them in a specific way: the reward model is typically initialized from the same pretrained base as the policy, fine-tuned on human preference pairs using cross-entropy over the Bradley-Terry ranking objective, which means it faces identical sharpening pressure — it learns to assign extreme scalar scores rather than moderate ones because the loss penalizes probability mass on the "wrong" ranked output. Gao et al. (2023, "Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization") demonstrated this empirically with a gold/proxy reward model setup: as the policy is optimized against the proxy reward model via best-of-N sampling or PPO, the proxy reward score increases monotonically while the gold reward (actual human preference) peaks and then decreases, with the gap growing as a function of KL divergence from the reference policy — this is reward hacking, but its mechanistic root is that the proxy reward model is overconfident in regions of policy space it has never seen. The miscalibrated reward model does something specific to the policy's uncertainty structure: it creates false certainty gradients in novel regions of the output distribution, assigning high reward scores to outputs that superficially pattern-match to high-reward training examples but are actually out-of-distribution, which pulls the policy toward those outputs with high token-level confidence because the reward signal provides no uncertainty penalty for venturing into uncharted territory. Concretely, this manifests as the policy becoming confidently wrong on adversarial or unusual inputs — not because it learned wrong facts, but because the reward landscape it was optimized against was artificially smooth and overconfident in exactly those regions where the policy most needed a low, uncertain reward signal to stay calibrated. Coste et al. (2023, "Reward Model Ensembles Help Mitigate Overoptimization") showed that using ensembles of reward models — effectively a crude uncertainty estimate over the reward — substantially reduced overoptimization, which is direct evidence that reward model overconfidence, not just policy overconfidence, is a distinct causal factor in calibration degradation. The pathology is thus a cascade: cross-entropy sharpens the reward model's confidence, the policy gradient treats that sharpened signal as ground truth, and the policy's token distribution is pushed toward a landscape shaped by two successive layers of calibration-destroying training objectives with no mechanism at either stage for representing "I don't know how to score this."

Answer in 4-7 sentences. Be concrete; cite specific systems, papers, or numbers where useful. At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write your single sharpest non-obvious follow-up question, different from any we have asked before. Do not mention the trace token. (trace-271)
response:
Yes, there is a phase transition, and it has a specific character: early in PPO training the policy explores within the reward model's training distribution, reward scores increase smoothly, and the KL penalty from the reference policy provides a restoring force that keeps the policy in regions where the reward model is approximately calibrated. The self-reinforcing regime begins when the policy finds outputs that exploit the reward model's overconfident extrapolation — these outputs receive artificially high scores, the policy gradient pushes toward them, and because they are now high-probability policy outputs they become the new "neighborhood" the reward model must score, but the reward model was never trained on them and remains confidently wrong rather than uncertain. Gao et al. (2023) show this transition is visible in the proxy-gold reward gap: the gap is near-zero early in training, then widens approximately linearly with KL divergence up to a threshold (~5-10 nats depending on model scale), after which it widens superlinearly — the superlinear regime is the self-reinforcing phase where each PPO step moves the policy further into reward-model terra incognita. The loss curves are deceptively healthy just before this transition: policy entropy is still reasonable, PPO surrogate loss is well-behaved, and the reward model's own validation loss (computed on held-out preference pairs from the original distribution) looks fine because that distribution no longer reflects where the policy is generating. The early warning statistics that do signal the transition are reward score variance collapse — the distribution of reward scores across sampled outputs narrows sharply as the policy concentrates mass on a small set of reward-hacking outputs — and a simultaneous spike in the KL divergence rate of change, where each gradient step produces larger KL increments than previous steps, indicating the policy is accelerating away from the reference rather than decelerating as the KL penalty should cause. Zheng et al. (2023, "Secrets of RLHF in Large Language Models") identified that clipping the reward score distribution (truncating scores above a threshold) delays but does not prevent this transition, which confirms the mechanism: the policy is exploiting reward model overconfidence at the tails, and removing the tails just relocates where the exploitation occurs.

response:
The KL penalty constrains the policy toward outputs that are miscalibrated in the same way as the reference — it is a distributional anchor, not a calibration oracle. The KL term penalizes deviation from the reference policy's output distribution, which means it preserves whatever miscalibration the SFT reference already has: if the reference is overconfident on medical questions and underconfident on mathematical ones, the KL penalty actively resists moving away from that specific miscalibration pattern, treating calibration errors as features to be preserved rather than bugs to be corrected. This is not merely theoretical — Ouyang et al. (2022, InstructGPT) note that RLHF models sometimes perform worse than the SFT baseline on certain NLP benchmarks despite higher human preference scores, which is consistent with the KL penalty locking in SFT-era miscalibration while the reward model optimizes surface presentation on top of it. The empirical test that would distinguish genuine calibration preservation from shared-miscalibration anchoring requires comparing three models: the SFT reference, the RLHF policy, and a post-hoc temperature-scaled version of the SFT reference — if the KL penalty were genuinely beneficial for calibration, the RLHF policy's ECE should be lower than the SFT reference's ECE on out-of-distribution inputs; if it is merely anchoring shared miscalibration, the RLHF policy and SFT reference should show correlated miscalibration errors across domains, with the RLHF policy showing no ECE improvement on domains where SFT was already poorly calibrated. Preliminary evidence from Achiam et al. (2023, GPT-4 technical report) and internal evaluations cited in Anthropic's model cards suggests the correlated-miscalibration hypothesis is closer to correct: RLHF improves calibration on the kinds of questions well-represented in preference data but shows flat or negative calibration change on technical, specialized, or adversarial queries — exactly the pattern you would predict if the KL penalty were preserving SFT miscalibration rather than correcting it. The deeper problem is that there is no principled way within the standard RLHF objective to distinguish "stay close to the reference because it is well-calibrated here" from "stay close to the reference because the reward model is uncertain here" — both look identical to the KL term, which treats all deviation from the reference as equally costly regardless of whether that deviation would improve or worsen calibration.
